seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: I have instructed my solicitors of that trust to remit you on the 25 September £14-0-0 equivalent at present rate of frs 621 x £1-0-0. Please do not discuss this point in your reply. The outstanding amount for our collective hotel expenses I shall make up separately.
Up to now (Saturday, 11 a.m.) there is no letter or wire or remittance. The following is the budget

I have at present about enough in my pocket to reach Monday forenoon by careful steering. I do not purpose trying to borrow anything from the people to whom you introduced me as it would be fatal, I suppose, to any prospects I may have here.

If nothing arrives here before the afternoon of Monday I shall begin by selling or pawning our two watches and if it turns out that Huebsch, Pinker, Quinn and Co are not going to give me any money I shall be compelled, of course, to look for any kind of a position here in order to keep us all from starving – in which case Ulysses must be postponed.
I saw Bradley who says perhaps he may be able to see about a bed and bedding.
It is impossible to write, my ear being always strained for the feet of phantom postmen.
Kind regards to Mrs Pound and yourself

div.note: We infer the date of 24 July 1920 from the postmark on the associated envelope and from JJ’s mention in this letter of “now … Saturday.” 24 July 1920 was a Saturday.

JJ and family had arrived in Paris from Trieste circa 8-9 July 1920, staying first at a hotel at 9 rue de l’Université, Paris 7e. By 15 July, they were installed at 5 rue de l’Assomption, in Passy, near the Bois de Boulogne, courtesy of the Russian-born Ludmila Bloch-Savitsky (1881-1957) and her husband, a railroad chief engineer, Marcel Bloch (1881-1951), who offered JJ the flat rent-free for three months. “It was a small three-room flat, with two bedrooms facing the street, a storage room, and a tiny kitchen. In this ‘matchbox,’ as Joyce called it, the family stayed from July 15 to November 1” (Ellmann, JJ 487). JJ’s initial plan was to stay in Paris for three months to finish the “Circe” and “Eumaeus” episodes of Ulysses (LI 142). As it turned out, he remained there for twenty years. Bloch-Savitsky, whom Pound had urged to read and translate JJ’s A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, published her French translation, Dedalus; Portrait de l’artiste jeune par lui-même, in 1924 with Éditions de la Sirène of Paris.

JJ learned in May 1919 from the London solicitors Monro, Saw & Company that an anonymous donor who had gifted him £200 in 1917 had decided to settle on him £5,000 in war loan securities in a trust fund, the interest to be paid at five percent as a modest but independent income (Mary T. Reynolds, “Joyce and Miss Weaver,” James Joyce Quarterly, vol. 19, no. 4 [Summer 1982]: 380-81). Harriet Shaw Weaver (1876-1961) revealed herself as the donor in a letter to JJ dated 6 July 1919 (John Firth, “Harriet Weaver’s Letters to James Joyce 1915-1920,” Studies in Bibliography, vol. 20 [1967]: 181-82). Weaver’s solicitors told JJ that she admired his “searching piercing spirit, [his] scorching truth, the power and startling penetration of [his] ‘intense instants of imagination’ [and his] very unusual and astonishing power of expression” (LII 445).

Despite JJ’s request, Pound did discuss the point in his 2 August 1920 letter: “I shall take it as an extremely unfriendly act if you instruct your damn solicitors to do anything of the sort; which wd. be pure imbecility on the one hand, you being sure to need the cash three weeks later; and damn’d unpleasant of you on the other, as I should like to make at least that small contribution to the running expenses of Ulysses” (Pound/Joyce 183). Pound was being his usual generous self in helping JJ and his family to get by in their first weeks in Paris. In mid-July 1920, JJ told Harriet Shaw Weaver that any result of his own current efforts “is all due to Mr Pound’s energy,” and wrote his literary agent J.B. Pinker: “I am enabled to exist [until 20 July] thanks to the kindness of Mr Pound” (LI 143).

A proper bed for JJ’s lanky son Giorgio had been lacking, and the young man had evidently been staying at a hotel, with tips for the chambermaid and the serving-man. Jenny Serruys (1886-1983), a wartime Red Cross nurse and French literary figure who was an early candidate for translating A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man into French, provided a portable bed for Giorgio after being urged by Pound, who felt that he himself was getting too involved in “sheets and truckle-beds for the errors J.J.’s his misspent premalthusian youth” (Pound/Joyce 180). Although Serruys did not translate A Portrait, she did produce a French translation of Exiles (Les Exilés) which was published under her married name J.S. Bradley by nrf Gallimard in Paris in 1950.

With Pound’s assistance, JJ was encountering the Paris literary scene and its actors, including André Spire, Sylvia Beach, Adrienne Monnier, Fritz Vanderpyl, Julien Benda, and others (Ellmann, JJ 485-89; Pound/Joyce 180-82).

note.p: JJ was expecting royalties and sums from various sources, and urging his London literary agent J.B. Pinker (prob. 1862 or 1863-1922) to collect these (LI 143). On 3 June 1920, Pinker had sent on £15, minus commission, for the Spanish translation rights of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, and on 17 June wrote that he was negotiating a contract for the book version of Ulysses with JJ’s American publisher, B.W. Huebsch (1876-1964) (John Firth, “James Pinker to James Joyce, 1915–1920,” Studies in Bibliography 21 [1968]: 223-24). JJ hoped that Huebsch would advance him royalties on Ulysses, and Huebsch mentioned the possibility of £25 on account of future royalties (LIII 12). But Pound saw no chance of “Huebsch paying £££ advance on mss. he hadn’t seen” (Pound/Joyce 183). In the end, Huebsch would not risk publishing Ulysses without changes, and JJ would not expurgate.

JJ was also hoping that the New York lawyer John Quinn (1870-1924), a collector of modern art and literary manuscripts, would make a further payment on his purchase of the Ulysses manuscript. On 5 February 1920 Quinn had cabled JJ an advance of 3,000 lire or $153.85. On 15 August 1920 he sent another payment of 3,400 francs or $250, with an additional sum of 1,400 francs in the fall of 1920 (Myron Schwartzman, “‘Quinnigan’s Quake!’ John Quinn’s Letters to James Joyce, 1916-1920,” Bulletin of Research in the Humanities, vol. 81, no. 2 [Summer 1978]: 237, 241-42, 245-46, 254, 258). For a full account, see JJ to Pound, 24 July 1917, notes.

div.note: William Aspenwall Bradley (1878-1939) was an American writer and critic and the fiancé of Jenny Serruys, who located a portable bed for JJ’s son Giorgio during their first weeks in Paris (see note 4 above). JJ liked Bradley and discussed aspects of Ulysses with him (Ellmann, JJ 487-88). Around 1923, Bradley and Serruys founded the William A. Bradley Literary Agency in Paris and represented important authors on both sides of the Atlantic. In The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas (1933), Gertrude Stein referred to Bradley as “the friend and comforter of Paris authors” (Selected Writings of Gertrude Stein, ed. Carl Van Vechten [New York: Random House, 1946], 200).
